vignette:
She is 24, a Latin American woman who comes to therapy speaking in a careful, measured way, as if she is still checking whether it is safe to say too much. Before the attack, she describes her life as ordinary and busy: long shifts at a warehouse, afternoons spent texting her mother, weekends with cousins, and an ongoing sense that she was trying to get ahead by sheer effort. She is single and not in a hurry to date, saying she has always preferred to keep her life small and manageable. She has a routine, and she relies on routine.

That changed when the bombing happened near the bus stop she used after work. She had just finished her shift and was waiting with other commuters when the explosion shook the street. In the first seconds, she does not understand what has happened; she remembers a flash, a pressure in her chest, and then the sound becoming strangely distant. People were screaming, running, dropping bags. She hits the ground and covers her head, convinced at first that another blast is coming. The smell of smoke and dust stays with her. She remembers looking at a shoe on the pavement and thinking, with a kind of stunned disbelief, that someone had been standing in it moments before. For days afterward, she cannot stop returning to that image.

In the aftermath, she moves through the world as if her body no longer belongs to her. At work she keeps going because she needs the money, but she is jumpy every time a pallet bangs against metal or a forklift backfires. Loud noises make her shoulders jerk before she can stop them. She begins arriving early so she can choose a spot near an exit and avoid standing in crowded places. Her coworkers notice that she has become quieter. She says little during breaks and scans the windows without realizing it. If someone mentions news from another city or an incident on the radio, she feels her stomach tighten and her hands go cold.

Sleep is one of the first things to unravel. She lies down exhausted and wakes after a few hours with her heart racing, certain for a moment that she is hearing the explosion again. Sometimes she dreams of the street, but in the dreams she cannot move or call out. When she wakes, she checks the locks, then checks them again, and again, until she feels only briefly settled. She starts sleeping with the television on because silence makes her think too much. Even then, she wakes to imagined sounds and lies rigid in bed, listening. The mornings are heavy. She drags herself through showers and breakfasts she does not taste.

She notices that her mind keeps replaying the day in fragments, not as a full story but as flashes: the dust cloud, a man bleeding from the arm, a child crying, the sensation of her own breath coming too fast. These images arrive when she is trying to work, when she is on the bus, when she is alone in the shower. Sometimes she finds herself back at the bus stop in her mind and has to shake herself out of it. She avoids walking past the site of the attack, even if it means a longer route. She stops going out after work unless someone is with her. She does not say it aloud, but she feels embarrassed by how much space fear has taken over her life.

Her family wants her to “move on,” and she tries to explain that nothing about her feels fully steady anymore. She is more irritable than before and then feels guilty for snapping at her younger brother or for not returning her mother’s calls right away. She has less patience, less interest in the small social routines she used to enjoy. At the same time, she is not numb exactly; she is too alert, too easily startled, too aware of the possibility that harm can arrive without warning. She says that before the attack she believed danger was something that happened somewhere else. Now she believes danger can be hidden anywhere, and that belief follows her everywhere.

Over time, she does develop a few ways of coping. She keeps her phone charged, avoids the news when she can, and listens to music on the bus so she does not have to listen to the city as closely. On good days she is able to focus on the rhythm of warehouse work, the stacking and sorting, the physicality of it. She says the repetitive motion helps her stay in the present, though even there her eyes still track the exits. She is proud of herself for continuing to work, but she also describes feeling as if she is doing so on borrowed energy, as if each day requires more effort than the one before.

In session she speaks about the attack with a flatness that contrasts with the intensity of what she describes. It is only gradually that her tears appear, often when she talks about ordinary things that were interrupted: the half-eaten snack in her bag, the text she never sent, the plan to meet a cousin that evening. What remains with her most is not just fear, but the sense that the world can change in an instant and that her body has not stopped waiting for it to happen again.
